title: Eliminate EUV in the array: maskless DUV interference lithography lattices
idea: The cell array is a perfectly periodic lattice, so expose the wordline, bitline and capacitor-hole layers with a three-beam 193 nm immersion interference tool (no reticle, no projection optics), then halve or quarter the pitch with ALD spacers. One coarse DUV trim mask removes the lattice at array edges, where conventional DUV patterns the periphery.
why: Litho and capital (fact 4): replaces 5-7 EUV exposures with a reticle-free tool costing ~$10-20M vs ~$200M per EUV scanner; estimated 15-25% wafer-cost cut and no single-supplier EUV dependence.

title: Eliminate the high-aspect-ratio capacitor etch with anodized alumina pores
idea: Deposit 2-3 um of aluminium over the landing pads, pre-dimple it with a shallow DUV-defined seed lattice, and anodize it so self-ordered hexagonal nanopores grow straight down onto each pad; ALD TiN/ZrO2/TiN then lines the pores. No resist, no hard mask and no HAR plasma etch are used for the storage node.
why: Facts 1 and 4: electrochemical pores reach AR >150:1 in a wet bath, enabling Cs ~8 fF, and remove the slowest, costliest etch module and its hard-mask stack; capacitor-module capex down an estimated ~40%.

title: Eliminate the silicon wafer: DRAM on Gen-8.5 display glass panels
idea: Build 12-16 tiers of oxide-TFT gain cells at F~0.5 um on 2.2 x 2.5 m glass in under-used LCD/OLED fabs, which already own panel-scale litho, sputter and PECVD. One panel has ~60x the area of a 300 mm wafer, so even at coarse F it holds ~3-7 TB of capacity-tier memory behind a CXL-style controller.
why: Capital and crucible chokepoint: display-fab capex per m2 is ~50-100x lower than a DRAM fab, with no Czochralski silicon, quartz crucible or EUV; targets ~$1-3/GB for a slower (~100 ns) tier that frees real DRAM for hot data.

title: Eliminate one-crystal-per-wafer: kerfless epitaxial lift-off from reusable parent wafers
idea: Grow a 50-100 um device-grade epitaxial silicon layer on a double-porous-silicon release layer atop a Czochralski parent wafer, bond it to a reclaimed-silicon carrier and cleave; the parent is re-porosified and reused 20-50 times.
why: Scarce resource and capital: cuts crystal pulls and high-purity quartz crucible consumption ~20x per wafer start, de-risking the Spruce Pine chokepoint; epi reactors are commodity, US-buildable tools.

title: Eliminate the quartz crucible: electromagnetic cold-crucible silicon crystal growth
idea: Melt silicon in a water-cooled segmented copper crucible where RF induction heats the charge and pushes the melt off the wall (skull melting), so it never touches quartz, and pull 300 mm crystals from it under a magnetic field; oxygen is added only by controlled gas doping.
why: Removes the >80% Spruce Pine high-purity quartz dependence outright and tightens interstitial-oxygen control (fewer slip and precipitate yield losses); cold-crucible casting already exists for solar silicon.

title: Eliminate the ballroom cleanroom: wafers live inside a vacuum backbone
idea: Connect every process tool to a linear vacuum or nitrogen wafer highway so wafers never meet fab air from start to finish; the building becomes an ISO-8 warehouse without raised floors or giant make-up air handlers.
why: Capital and time: the cleanroom shell and HVAC are ~20-30% of fab construction cost and a large energy share; could cut build time by about a year and total capex ~15%.

title: Eliminate resist and etch: imprinted inhibitor molecules steer area-selective ALD
idea: Nanoimprint a monolayer of ALD-inhibitor molecules (e.g., alkylsilane SAMs) in the negative pattern, then grow the film only where it is uninhibited, so the layer is patterned additively in one deposition with no resist coat, exposure, develop, etch or strip.
why: Collapses a ~5-tool, 8-12 step patterning loop into 2 steps for semi-critical layers; applied to ~15 layers it trims fab tool count ~10% and cuts chemistry and water per layer.

title: Eliminate step-and-repeat: whole-wafer single-shot roll nanoimprint
idea: Roll a flexible replica stamp across the full 300 mm wafer in one pass, patterning every die at once in UV-cured resist; distortion is corrected by thermally actuated zones in the stamp frame, mapped against wafer alignment marks.
why: Throughput and capital: one ~$5M imprint station replaces a scanner for array layers at >100 wafers/hour, with no stitching, projection optics or light source.

title: Eliminate periphery and product layout from array wafers: universal lattice wafers
idea: Fabricate wafers that hold nothing but an endless, product-agnostic cell lattice (no decoders, sense amps or I/O), then hybrid-bond them wafer-to-wafer onto separately made logic wafers that define product, banking and die boundaries; die size is chosen at dicing.
why: Facts 4 and 7: the array fab needs ~40% fewer masks and no product-specific reticles, runs one recipe at full utilization, and periphery moves to a cheaper logic process; ~20-30% cost-per-bit gain.

title: Eliminate the binary bit: ternary-charge cells give 58% more bits per mask
idea: Store three charge levels per cell (0, half and full VBLH) and read them with a two-reference successive-approximation sense amplifier; pairs of cells hold 9 states and encode 3 bits.
why: Litho and capital: ~50% more bits from the same mask stack and wafer, a 'free node' without EUV, paid for with sense margin and a higher refresh rate.

title: Eliminate ion implantation: junctions set by in-situ doped epitaxy and work functions
idea: Form access-transistor and periphery source/drains by selective in-situ doped epitaxy and set thresholds with gate-metal work-function stacks and dipole layers, so the flow needs no implanter and no implant masks.
why: Removes ~8-12 non-critical masks plus implanters and activation anneals, shortening cycle time ~10% and lowering tool capex; also removes random dopant fluctuation from the leakage tail.

title: Eliminate tungsten and its liner: barrierless molybdenum buried wordlines
idea: Fill buried-wordline trenches with molybdenum deposited by ALD/CVD directly on the gate dielectric with no TiN barrier, and spend the freed liner volume on conductor.
why: Scarce resource: swaps tungsten (China ~80%) for molybdenum mined in the US; removes a liner deposition per metallization and lowers wordline resistance ~30%, allowing thinner, easier wordlines.

title: Eliminate helium from the fab: hydrogen backside cooling and tracer leak checks
idea: Replace helium backside gas on etch and CVD electrostatic chucks with low-pressure hydrogen or forming gas (higher thermal conductivity, sealed with flow monitoring), and replace helium mass-spec leak checks with 5% hydrogen tracer detection.
why: Scarce resource: Qatar's ~30% helium share is offline; fab helium use could drop >80%, removing a supply shock that can idle etch fleets.

title: Eliminate multi-year construction: factory-built containerized fab modules
idea: Build standardized 2,500 wafer-per-month array-line modules, with tools pre-installed in sealed clean containers with integrated utilities, in a shipyard-style factory, and bolt them onto an on-site utility spine one module at a time.
why: Capital and time: fab-to-first-wafer from 3-5 years to ~12-18 months, and capacity added in $1-2B steps instead of $15B, matching scarcity-driven demand.

title: Eliminate up-front tool capex: pay-per-wafer-pass equipment ownership by vendors
idea: Tool vendors own, install and maintain the equipment in a new US DRAM fab and bill per wafer pass with guaranteed uptime; the memory company carries only the building and labor, and vendors refurbish tools for the next node.
why: Capital intensity (depreciation ~55% of wafer cost): turns fixed cost into variable cost, lowers the entry barrier for new US makers and cuts downturn losses.

title: Eliminate CMP: subtractive metal patterning plus flowable self-planarizing dielectric
idea: Pattern bitlines and landing pads by direct etch of blanket Ru or Mo instead of damascene, then gap-fill with flowable SiOC that self-levels and is etched back to an optical endpoint, removing chemical-mechanical polish steps.
why: Removes ~10-20 CMP steps, slurry and much ultrapure-water use plus dishing-driven yield loss; ~5-8% fewer tools.

title: Eliminate liquid drying and support lattices: vapor-HF release plus supercritical CO2
idea: Remove the capacitor mold oxide with vapor-phase HF and rinse/dry in supercritical CO2, so tall pillars never see a liquid-vapor meniscus and need none of the nitride support lattices added today to stop leaning and stiction.
why: Fact 1: removes 2-3 support-layer deposition/litho/etch loops and lets AR rise from ~70 to ~115:1 without collapse (~50% more Cs), while cutting water use.

title: Eliminate access-transistor lithography: grow vertical nanowire channels from catalysts
idea: Place catalyst dots with a block-copolymer lattice (no mask), grow vertical single-crystal Si nanowires by vapor-liquid-solid epitaxy with a CMOS-friendly catalyst (Al or Cu-silicide), then wrap them in ALD gate stacks to form 4F2 vertical access transistors.
why: Facts 2 and 4: removes the EUV-class active-area and channel etch masks; bottom-up wires have smooth sidewalls and low trap density, tightening the leakage tail.

title: Eliminate deposited channels in 3D tiers: ion-cut transfer of single-crystal films
idea: For each 3D tier, bond and Smart-Cut a 20-50 nm single-crystal Si film from a donor wafer onto the finished tier below, build the lateral transistors at <=500 C with laser anneal, and reuse the donor dozens of times.
why: Fact 2: gives 3D DRAM a crystalline lateral transistor without Si/SiGe superlattice epitaxy and its 26+ tier stack etch, cutting epi tool count and stack-etch risk.

title: Eliminate the access transistor: threshold-selector-gated capacitors in BEOL crossbars
idea: Put a two-terminal threshold switch (an ovonic or NbOx selector tuned for femtoamp-class off-current) in series with a MIM capacitor at each wordline/bitline crossing, forming a 1S1C 4F2 cell built entirely in back-end layers and stacked 8+ high.
why: Removes the whole front-end access-transistor module (most critical masks) and stacks with one mask pair per tier; cost per bit could drop 2-3x if selector leakage reaches ~1 fA.

title: Eliminate the fab's lithography: DNA-origami templated nanoscale memory assembly
idea: DNA origami tiles bind to a coarse DUV-patterned wafer and place carbon-nanotube transistors and metal-oxide nanoparticle capacitors with ~5 nm precision, after which ALD locks and metallizes the assembly; the cell layout is coded in DNA sequence, not masks.
why: Ultimate litho elimination: sub-10 nm cells from a fab of wet benches, coarse litho and ALD; speculative, but would cut capital per bit by >10x.

title: Eliminate CVD electrodes: electroless ruthenium plating inside capacitor holes
idea: Seed the capacitor mold holes with a palladium-activated monolayer and electrolessly plate conformal Ru bottom and top electrodes from a wet bath, replacing CVD/ALD TiN.
why: Capital: plating cells cost a fraction of ALD/CVD chambers at higher throughput, and Ru's higher work function cuts dielectric leakage, allowing thinner high-k and more Cs.

title: Eliminate periphery photomasks: maskless micromirror digital lithography for relaxed layers
idea: Expose the 20-30 relaxed periphery and implant-class layers with a digital-micromirror maskless writer (as used in advanced packaging) pushed to 248/193 nm, so no reticles are bought, stored or requalified per product.
why: Capital and agility: removes ~$3-8M of masks per product revision and cuts new-variant ramp time from months to days.

title: Eliminate laser fuse repair: on-die BIST and BIRA blow antifuses
idea: The die runs its own march test and built-in redundancy analysis at wafer sort and programs repair electrically into antifuses, so the laser-repair tools, their test insertion and external repair-analysis servers disappear. The host sees an ordinary DDR5 or HBM3E die.
why: Test capital: removes laser repair and a repair-test insertion (~5-10% of back-end test cost) with zero interface change.

title: Eliminate burn-in ovens: on-die heaters stress dies during wafer sort
idea: Add a thin metal heater mesh under each die and use internal charge pumps to apply elevated VPP/VARY while heating dies to ~125 C at the prober, screening infant mortality without package burn-in ovens. Shipped parts are standard DDR5/HBM3E; the heaters are left floating.
why: Removes burn-in boards, ovens and hours of cycle time, and screens before packaging so bad dies never consume HBM stacking cost.

title: Eliminate probe cards: contactless whole-wafer optical power and RF readout
idea: Each die carries a small photovoltaic cell and a near-field RF backscatter antenna in the scribe; a high-intensity LED array powers every die on the wafer to run internal BIST, results are read wirelessly in parallel, and the test circuitry is cut off at dicing. DDR/HBM pads are never touched and the product interface is unchanged.
why: Probe cards and ATE channels are a major memory-test capex line; parallel contactless sort tests thousands of dies per shot and leaves hybrid-bond pads pristine.

title: Eliminate scrap from partial dies: sell them as JEDEC 24Gb parts
idea: Design 32 Gb DDR5 dies so any one quarter of the array can be fused off; dies with a dead quadrant are configured as the non-binary 24 Gb density already in the DDR5 spec and built into standard 24/48/96 GB modules that hosts already support.
why: Yield and capital: recovers ~5-15% of dies that would be scrapped during a ramp, adding effective wafer capacity without a single new tool.

title: Eliminate signal TSVs between HBM core dies: inductive-coupling vertical links
idea: Replace the thousands of signal TSVs in core dies with on-chip coil pairs that couple data and clock between neighboring thinned dies, keeping only a few large power vias; the base die still presents a standard HBM3E/HBM4 PHY to the GPU.
why: Fact 6: removes most deep-via etch, liner, Cu fill, reveal and micro-bumps, recovering part of the ~3x area-per-bit tax and the 20-30% stack yield loss.

title: Eliminate whole-stack scrap: a hot-spare core die inside each HBM stack
idea: Bond 13 core dies for a 12-high HBM3E stack; the base die tests each layer after bonding and steers a failed die's channels to the spare through a crossbar, so the GPU sees a standard 12-high device.
why: Fact 6: stack losses of 20-30% (one bad die kills the stack) fall to a few percent, worth far more than the ~8% extra die cost.

title: Eliminate per-product mask sets: one array die personalized late
idea: Design a single core array with interchangeable top-metal and fuse options so the same front-end wafers become DDR5 x4/x8, LPDDR5X or HBM core dies by choosing last-via masks late in the line. Each product still meets its unchanged JEDEC interface.
why: Capital: one front-end mask set instead of three (~$15-30M each with EUV), and output can swing between markets mid-flow, lifting fab utilization.

title: Eliminate EUV entirely: 4F2 vertical-channel cells at relaxed DUV pitch
idea: Move to a 4F2 vertical-channel-transistor cell but hold F at ~15 nm, which matches the bit area of today's 6F2 at 12 nm and is reachable with immersion DUV plus self-aligned quadruple/octuple patterning. Output is an ordinary DDR5/HBM core die.
why: Fact 4: zero EUV layers at bit-density parity, removing ~$1B+ of scanners per 100k wafers/month and the single-supplier dependency.

title: Eliminate the capacitor-hole mask: block-copolymer self-assembly guided by landing pads
idea: Coat a cylinder-forming block copolymer over the landing-pad topography so it self-assembles into a hexagonal hole array registered to the pads, and use it directly as the hard-mask template for capacitor holes. The die and its DDR5/HBM interface are unchanged.
why: Replaces one EUV or 2-3 DUV multipatterning exposures with a spin and bake, and tightens hole-CD uniformity, narrowing Cs variation.

title: Eliminate retention-test hours: profile weak cells silently inside refresh
idea: Skip the long hot pause and retention tests on ATE; the die uses part of each JEDEC tRFC window to read-compare sample rows at stretched intervals, learns which rows sit in the leakage tail and refreshes them more often internally. The host still issues standard REF commands.
why: Facts 3 and 4: retention screening is among the longest ATE steps; moving it into the field cuts test time ~20-30% and keeps weak-cell dies instead of repairing or scrapping them.

title: Eliminate spare rows, columns and fuses: DDR5 on-die ECC absorbs defects
idea: Remove most row/column redundancy and fuse banks; single-cell hard faults stay in place for the existing DDR5 on-die SEC ECC and Error-Check-and-Scrub to correct, with a small spare pool kept only for cluster faults. The DDR5 interface and its ECS reporting are unchanged.
why: Frees ~3-5% of die area and removes fuse-programming test time, a few percent more bits per wafer at no tool cost.

title: Eliminate thick-oxide I/O masks: co-packaged legacy-node DDR5 PHY chiplet
idea: Strip the I/O transistors, ESD and DLL from the DRAM die so its process needs only one gate oxide, and put the DDR5 PHY on a tiny 40 nm chiplet stacked face-to-face in the same FBGA package. Module pinout and timing stay JEDEC DDR5.
why: Removes ~3-5 masks (dual oxide, I/O implants, thick metal) and ~5-8% die area from the array process, cutting wafer cost per bit.

title: Eliminate leading-edge logic for HBM base dies: depreciated 28 nm US fabs
idea: Make HBM3E/HBM4-compatible base dies in fully depreciated 28-40 nm US logic fabs, using wider, slower internal channels to the core dies and a 28 nm PHY tuned to the JEDEC data rate. The GPU sees a standard HBM stack.
why: Capital and U.S. manufacturability: avoids competing for scarce 5/3 nm wafers; base-die wafer cost falls ~5-10x with near-zero depreciation.

title: Eliminate the pulse-purge ALD bottleneck: rotary spatial ALD for capacitor dielectrics
idea: Deposit the ZrO2/Al2O3/ZrO2 capacitor stack on a rotating platen that carries wafers through separated precursor and oxidant zones with long dwell for deep holes, instead of time-sequenced pulse-purge chambers. Device and DDR/HBM interface are unchanged.
why: ALD is among the most numerous DRAM tool types; spatial ALD runs ~5-10x faster per wafer, shrinking ALD tool count and floor space.

title: Eliminate CD-variation rework: per-bank voltage trims absorb multipatterning spread
idea: Instead of tightening process windows with more metrology, rework and scrap, trim each bank's VPP, VBLH and sense timing at sort so slow or leaky banks from DUV multipatterned arrays still meet JEDEC tRCD/tRAS and refresh specs. Host-visible timing is unchanged.
why: Allows looser overlay and CD specs (and so DUV instead of EUV) for a few trim fuses; estimated +5-10% yield and fewer inline metrology and rework passes.

title: Eliminate the tall capacitor: short storage nodes plus offset-cancelling sense amps
idea: Halve capacitor height (AR ~35:1, Cs ~2.5 fF) and recover margin with offset-cancelled, bitline-isolated sense amplifiers and shorter bitlines, absorbing the extra refresh inside the existing DDR5 refresh budget. The die still runs standard DDR5 timings.
why: Fact 1: halves the hardest etch, removes support-lattice steps and pillar-collapse loss; capacitor-module cost down ~30-40%, partly paid back in sense-amp area.

title: Eliminate die-by-die thermocompression bonders: wafer-on-wafer HBM core stacking
idea: Hybrid-bond whole core-die wafers on top of each other and dice finished stacks, replacing hundreds of slow pick-and-place TCB bonds per wafer with one bond per layer; the base die still speaks standard HBM3E/HBM4.
why: Fact 6 and capital: removes the TCB bonder bottleneck that limits HBM output, with ~10x stacking throughput per tool; best paired with spare-die repair to offset compounded yield.

title: Eliminate backgrinding waste: laser subsurface slicing of HBM core wafers
idea: Before TSV reveal, focus an infrared laser through the wafer back side to write a cleave plane ~40 um below the devices (as laser slicing does for SiC), split the device layer onto its carrier, and repolish the remaining ~700 um slab for reuse as monitor wafers or epitaxial donors. Resulting stacks are standard HBM.
why: HBM grinds away ~94% of each core wafer; reclaiming it cuts virgin-wafer demand (and Czochralski/crucible use) and removes grinding and CMP passes.

title: Eliminate per-die probe touchdowns: scribe-line test bus, one contact per wafer
idea: Wire every die to a shared power and serial test bus routed through the scribe lines to a few large edge pads; one touchdown powers all dies, each runs BIST and reports over the bus, and a fuse isolates shorted dies. Dicing cuts the bus away, leaving standard DDR5/HBM dies.
why: Replaces fine-pitch probe cards and multi-touchdown sort with one cheap contact; ~10x sort throughput and no probe marks on hybrid-bond pads.

title: Eliminate two EUV contact layers: self-aligned selective-epi bitline contacts and pads
idea: Grow bitline contacts and storage landing pads by selective Si/SiGe epitaxy only on exposed active silicon between spacer-defined lines, so they self-align to active areas instead of being printed with EUV contact masks. Output is an ordinary DDR5/HBM core die.
why: Fact 4: removes the two most overlay-critical EUV layers of current flows; self-aligned contacts tolerate DUV-grade overlay.

title: Eliminate greenfield fabs: convert shuttered 300 mm shells to DUV DDR4/DDR5
idea: Re-equip idle or shuttered US 300 mm shells with refurbished DUV-era DRAM tools to make 1x-nm DDR4, DDR5 and LPDDR4 for industrial, auto and PC markets, freeing leading-edge capacity for HBM. Parts are standard JEDEC devices.
why: Capital and time: ~1/3 the capex and ~1/2 the time of a greenfield fab, with no new interface for customers to qualify.

title: Eliminate idle EUV capex: national EUV pass utility shared by memory makers
idea: A government-backed consortium owns EUV scanners in one US litho hall beside several fabs and sells exposure passes; FOUPs move by sealed AMHS tunnel between companies, so no DRAM maker buys a full EUV fleet. Products remain standard DDR5/HBM.
why: Capital: lifts EUV utilization from ~60-70% to >90% across companies and lets new US entrants pay per exposure, cutting entry capex by billions.

title: Eliminate wide scribes: in-die test structures, plasma dicing, 10 um streets
idea: Move process-control monitors and alignment marks into dummy areas inside the die, shrink scribe streets from ~60-80 um to ~10 um, and singulate by plasma dicing; dies are unchanged JEDEC DDR5/HBM parts.
why: Adds ~3-6% gross dies per wafer and removes saw-kerf chipping on thin HBM dies, a free capacity gain.
